UX Writing Style Guide, CSA 2.0

Scope: This guide applies to text users see in CSA and communication with users outside CSA. Back-end terminology is up to the engineers and may differ from this guide.

CSA vibe: Trustworthy, professional, contemporary, and humane.
UX copy goals: Be clear. Be easy to use. Respect the user.

Guide:

Capitalization
Capitalize key words in buttons and headings, keep short connecting words such as “to” lowercase, and preserve acronyms. Follow exact approved labels.
Approved casing: Add to List, SEO Title, Send to your CMS, Creating Draft, and Revising Draft. Other status messages and full sentences use sentence case.
Yes: Add to List
Yes: SEO Title
No: Add To List
No: Add to list
No: ADD TO LIST
No: SEO title

Use familiar content language
Use language that is native to content creation, rather than creating new terminology.
Yes: Draft
No: Variant

Keep it concise
Use the shortest phrase required to describe a concept clearly. Avoid unnecessary words.
Yes: Format
Yes: Audience
No: Content Format
No: Target Audience

Describe usefulness, not technology
Avoid tech language because CSA is defined by its usefulness, not by the technology behind the scenes. Avoid tech jargon: its meaning changes rapidly and means different things to different people.
Yes: CSA will help format your content.
No: AI will help format your content.
No: LLMs will help format your content.

Keep the user involved and in control
Avoid language that suggests technology works independently of human involvement.
Yes: CSA is drafting.
Yes: CSA is revising.
No: CSA is generating.
No: CSA is creating.

Use flexible language for people and organizations
Be role- and company-agnostic. Use flexible language to describe users and their work wherever possible.
Yes: Send to your CMS
Yes: Hello, what are you working on today?
No: Send to your McClatchy website
No: Hello, what stories are you working on today?
No: Hello, what marketing copy are you working on today?

Stay platform agnostic
Do not assume the person is working with text content, such as articles.
Yes: CSA is digesting your sources
No: CSA is reading your article

Match the actual task
Text should match reality. Be trustworthy rather than engaging in theater.
Yes: Creating Draft [with gentle animation]
No: Checking your style [when it is not, at that moment, checking your style]

Speak, don’t shout
Use a calm, professional tone.
Yes: Creating Draft
No: Coming right up!

Use active voice
Make the action clear.
Yes: Creating Draft
No: Content is Drafting

The following concepts will become obsolete with CSA 2.0 and should be avoided:
No: Audience Variant
No: Platform Distribution
No: Platform Variant
No: Canonical Article
No: Research Draft
No: Market Audience
No: Geographic Audience
No: Market Variant
No: Content Scaling
No: CSA Combine

Product status labels: Creating Draft for new drafts; Revising Draft for revision requests.

Revision notes
Show entries newest first. A single revision has no numbered heading. With multiple revisions, show each entry’s original Revision N heading, so Revision 2 appears above Revision 1. Use semantic.color.text.primary (#404040) for these headings, matching New Draft. Show the completion date and time without a Revised label. Follow it with Requested Revision: and the exact original request, then Result: and the saved outcome. If no outcome was recorded, Result says “The result was not recorded.” The Revision History toggle keeps its count when there are multiple entries.
For a successful revision, Result describes the edit that actually happened, its location, and the resulting form. Lead the result with the action instead of repeating the request. For example: Converted the second paragraph into a bulleted list with two items; left all other content unchanged.
End completed-edit notes with “left all other content unchanged.” If nothing changed, say “Left all content unchanged.” Do not claim an edit happened based only on what was requested; use the saved before-and-after content. Preserve previously recorded outcomes.

Unapplied revisions
If a revision cannot be applied, use the same Requested Revision and Result fields. Preserve the exact original request under Requested Revision and show the saved refusal or limitation under Result. Ordinary unsupported requests explain what could not be applied and finish with “left all content unchanged.” The elephant refusal keeps its exact wording and includes the title of the story being revised. Never replace the draft with unrelated sample copy when a request is not recognized. A saved request by itself is not proof that its requested change happened.
